title: CI/CD pipelines, secrets, environment variables, approvals, and rollback
objectives: Define continuous integration as regularly integrating metadata source into a repository with automated builds and tests.
Keep secrets and org credentials out of Git; inject them as CI secrets or environment variables.
Place human approvals before production metadata deploy, distinct from Apex quality gates.
Describe rollback as a planned metadata action (fix-forward deploy, validated quick deploy, or package downgrade)—not git revert alone and not --ignore-errors.
diagnostic_question: A pipeline deploys LAB_ metadata to production using a connected-app secret committed in the repo, no approval job, and --ignore-errors so 'rollback is easier.' What do you change first?
definition: Continuous integration regularly merges Salesforce metadata source into version control and runs automated builds and tests. A CI/CD pipeline scripts retrieve/deploy/validate, tests, and promotions across environments. Secrets (JWT keys, refresh tokens, installation keys) must live in the CI secret store, not the DX project. Environment variables parameterize org aliases and test levels. Approvals are human go/no-go steps before production. Rollback is how you restore a safe metadata state after a bad deploy. ([Continuous Integration](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm); [project deploy start](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html); [project deploy validate](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_validate.html))
why_it_matters: A pipeline that commits secrets or ignore-errors on production is a security and consistency incident, not DevOps maturity. Interviewers want JWT/secrets outside Git, approvals separate from test gates, and rollback that is not a fairy-tale git revert of production.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a harbor lock. The pipeline is the sequence of chambers from Git basin to production harbor. Secrets are the lock keys—never painted on the hull (the repo). Environment variables are the tide tables for each harbor (which org, which test level). Approvals are the lock-keeper's hand on the gate before the last chamber. Rollback is reversing a chamber or sending a repair barge—not dynamiting the lock with ignore-errors. Quality gates (DEVOPS-006) are the depth sounder; they are not the keeper's signature.
deeper_explanation: Salesforce DX defines CI as developers regularly integrating code into a source repository with automated builds and tests so new code does not introduce bugs. DX integrates with third-party CI (Jenkins, CircleCI, Travis samples, and others). Sample repos exist for org development and package development models. ([Continuous Integration](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm))

Auth to Dev Hub and target orgs in CI uses secrets: JWT key files, consumer secrets, refresh tokens, package installation keys. These are environment variables or secret stores in the CI product—not files committed beside force-app. If a secret was committed, rotate it. Scratch orgs in CI should not receive personal data.

Approvals in this topic are pipeline promotions (a human must click before production metadata deploy), not Salesforce Flow approval processes. Quality gates can be fully automated; production still often needs a change-approval step. Validate then quick deploy (10-day job ID) is a way to separate long tests from the approved window. ([project deploy validate](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_validate.html))

Rollback: never --ignore-errors on production; it can leave an inconsistent org. A failed deploy with rollbackOnError (default in many tools) leaves the org as it was. After a successful bad deploy, git revert is only source truth—you still must deploy the reverted metadata (fix-forward) or install a previous package version. Destructive changes and data side effects may not reverse by redeploying old XML. Plan rollback in the release notes (DEVOPS-010).

mental_model.analogy: A harbor lock: pipeline chambers, secrets as keys not painted on the hull, environment variables as per-harbor tide tables, approvals as the lock-keeper, rollback as reversing a chamber or sending a repair barge—not dynamite (ignore-errors).
useful_mapping: CD → promoting the same artifact toward production
secret → JWT key, token, install key in CI store
environment variable → org alias, test level, API version per chamber
approval → human gate before production deploy
validate job ID → tests done in an upstream chamber, 10-day ticket
rollback → deploy last known good metadata or prior package version
ignore-errors → dynamite that can split the lock
where_it_breaks: Salesforce metadata deploy is not a container image you un-tag from a registry.
Some metadata and all business data will not roll back with a Git revert deploy.
DevOps Center is an official alternative UI; this lesson still uses CLI as the contract.
Vendor YAML is not Salesforce documentation.

claims.claim: CI is regularly integrating code into a source repository with automated builds and tests. Salesforce DX integrates with third-party CI tools and provides sample repos for org and package development models.
claims.validation: Continuous Integration in the Salesforce DX Developer Guide.

claims.claim: Never use --ignore-errors when deploying to production; partial success can leave an inconsistent org.
project deploy validate does not execute the deploy; the job ID is valid 10 days for project deploy quick. Do not use validate on sandboxes.
The CLI is the documented tool for development, continuous integration, and delivery, with version control as the source of truth.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: CI merges metadata often and runs automated tests. Secrets stay in the CI store as environment variables, not in Git. Approvals are humans before production. Rollback is deploy last-good or a previous package version. Never ignore-errors on production.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I sketch chambers: PR tests on scratch orgs, UAT deploy, validate on production, approval, quick deploy. I rotate any committed secret. I distinguish quality gates from CAB-style approval. I explain git revert still needs a metadata deploy and may not undo data or all deletes. I mention DX sample repos for org versus package models.

terminology.plain: Merge metadata source often and let machines test it.
terminology.precise: Developers regularly integrate code into a source repository; automated builds and tests run so new code does not introduce bugs.
terminology.example: Every LAB_ PR creates a scratch org, deploys, runs RunLocalTests, deletes the org.
terminology.non_example: A weekly manual change set with no tests.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Continuous delivery: promoting the same artifact onward.
terminology.boundary: Vendor YAML is not the Salesforce definition.

terminology.plain: The scripted chambers from Git to production.
terminology.precise: Automated jobs that test and deploy Salesforce metadata using CLI, wrapping org or package development models.
terminology.example: Jenkinsfile calling sf project deploy start with env-specific aliases.
terminology.non_example: A single developer deploying from a laptop with no record.
terminology.boundary: DevOps Center is an official alternative; CLI remains the contract here.

terminology.plain: A credential that must not be in the metadata repo.
terminology.precise: JWT private keys, consumer secrets, refresh tokens, package installation keys, and similar. Store in the CI secret manager.
terminology.example: SF_JWT_KEY as a masked CI secret used to auth the Dev Hub.
terminology.non_example: sfdx-project.json packageDirectories, which is not a secret.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Environment variable that is merely an org alias.
terminology.boundary: Rotate immediately if it was committed.

terminology.plain: A per-job setting such as which org or test level.
terminology.precise: Non-secret or secret-injected values that keep YAML generic: aliases, test levels, API versions.
terminology.non_example: Hard-coded production usernames in the Jenkinsfile committed to Git.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom metadata type records in the package.
terminology.boundary: Do not put private keys in unmasked job logs.

terminology.plain: A human go/no-go before production metadata deploy.
terminology.precise: Pipeline promotion approval, not a Salesforce record Approval Process. Distinct from automated quality gates.
terminology.example: Two reviewers click Approve on the production job after validate succeeds.
terminology.non_example: Apex test pass treated as legal approval.
terminology.boundary: Who may approve is a governance choice.

terminology.plain: Returning to a safe metadata state after a bad release.
terminology.precise: For a failed deploy, rely on transactional rollback—not ignore-errors. For a successful bad deploy, deploy last-known-good source or a previous package version. Git revert without deploy does nothing to the org.
terminology.example: Install unlocked package 1.3.0 after 1.4.0 misbehaves, if the version is still installable.
terminology.boundary: Deletes and some type changes may not reverse cleanly (DEVOPS-009).

terminology.plain: Use a successful validation job ID to deploy without rerunning those tests.
terminology.precise: After project deploy validate, project deploy quick within 10 days. Still overwrites corresponding metadata. Not for sandboxes.
terminology.example: Validate Monday, approve Friday, quick deploy the job ID.
terminology.non_example: Quick deploy of an unvalidated local folder.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: sf project deploy start --async, which is a different job.
terminology.boundary: If source changed after validate, re-validate.

terminology.plain: A deploy flag that can save some components and skip others.
terminology.precise: Never use when deploying to production; can leave an inconsistent production org.
terminology.example: A production job that omitted the flag and failed closed.
terminology.non_example: Using it as a rollback strategy.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: ignore-warnings, sometimes used when deleting already-absent components in CI.
terminology.boundary: ignore-warnings is not a license to hide compile errors.

interview_questions.question: What does Salesforce mean by continuous integration?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Developers regularly integrate metadata source into a repository. Automated builds and tests run so new code does not introduce bugs. DX plugs into third-party CI.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I mention sample repos for org versus package models. I use scratch orgs for PR proof. I keep secrets out. I do not claim a specific vendor is required. CLI is the lifecycle tool.
interview_questions.example: GitHub Actions: on pull_request, create scratch, deploy LAB_ source, run tests, delete.
tradeoffs: Org model vs package model CI

interview_questions.question: How do you handle secrets in a Salesforce pipeline?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: JWT keys, tokens, and package installation keys live in the CI secret store as masked environment variables. Never in Git. Rotate if leaked.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I separate aliases (config) from keys (secrets). I mask logs. I use a least-privilege CI user. I do not print sf org display that might show tokens. I still need API Enabled and Metadata deploy rights—those are permissions, not secrets.
interview_questions.example: SF_JWT_KEY file uploaded as a secret; Jenkins injects it at runtime.
follow_ups: Who owns the Dev Hub user?
weak_answer_warnings: Commit the key so CI works

interview_questions.question: Leadership wants auto-deploy to production on every main merge.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I can auto-deploy to a scratch or UAT. Production still needs quality gates and, if policy requires, a human approval. I will not add ignore-errors to make it always green.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I offer validate-on-main plus an approval job. I explain quick deploy for the window. I keep tests from DEVOPS-006. Some teams auto-prod for truly reversible unlocked packages—Needs verification of their risk appetite—but I would not default there for a shared enterprise org.
interview_questions.example: main merge deploys UAT; production waits for two approvers after validate.
tradeoffs: Package push upgrades vs source deploy

interview_questions.question: How do you roll back a successful bad production metadata deploy?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Deploy last-known-good Git or install a previous package version. GitHub revert without CLI does nothing to the org. Deletes may need destructive changes.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask what succeeded: additive fields are hard to undo if data exists. I prefer fix-forward if the bug is Apex. I never ignore-errors. I separate data restore. I mention 10-day validate IDs are not a rollback tool.
interview_questions.example: Install LabBoarding 1.3.0 after 1.4.0 broke a Flow; then retrieve to confirm Git matches.

interview_questions.question: Where do approvals sit relative to quality gates?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Gates are automated tests, coverage, analyzer. Approvals are humans after gates, before production deploy. Neither is a Flow approval process.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I would not make CAB re-run tests by hand if validate already did. I would not let approval skip failing tests. I store the validate job ID as evidence. I keep the approver list out of Apex.
interview_questions.example: Analyzer+tests green → manager approval → quick deploy.

interview_questions.question: How can validate/quick deploy fit a pipeline?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Run validate after UAT, keep the 10-day job ID, take the approval, then quick deploy in the freeze. Do not validate sandboxes.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: If metadata changes after validate, I re-validate. Quick deploy still overwrites metadata—it is not a rehearsal. I still monitor Deployment Status (DEVOPS-010). I do not use the job ID on a different org.
interview_questions.example: Monday validate against prod; Friday CAB; sf project deploy quick --job-id …
weak_answer_warnings: Validate UAT and quick-deploy production with that ID

interview_questions.question: CI prints a Salesforce access token in logs. Response?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Treat it as a leaked secret: revoke/rotate, mask the log step, purge logs if the vendor allows, stop printing org display in debug.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I check whether the token was in Git too. I reduce sf log level. I confirm the CI user cannot be used interactively from the leak. I add a pipeline test that fails if files look like keys.
interview_questions.example: Jenkins console showed sf org display output; rotate the refresh token and mask the step.
tradeoffs: Shared CI user vs per-env users
follow_ups: How long was the token valid?
weak_answer_warnings: Tokens in logs are fine because CI is internal

interview_questions.question: Design rollback for org-model versus package-model pipelines.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Org model: deploy a previous Git SHA. Package model: install a previous version if allowed. Both still need a CLI/org action. Neither undoes data by itself.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I keep last-good identifiers in the release ticket. Org-model rollbacks can be messy with profile XML. Package-model rollbacks depend on upgrade/downgrade rules—Needs verification per package type. I add destructive-change planning for deletes. I forbid ignore-errors as a fake rollback.
interview_questions.example: Org model: deploy tag release-2026-08-01. Package model: sf package install LabBoarding@1.3.0 --target-org prod (only if policy allows).
tradeoffs: Git SHA pinpoint vs package inventory
weak_answer_warnings: Same rollback as Docker image pull
